To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we identified 17 germline mutations among 100 early-onset breast cancers and that TP53 mutation testing should be offered to early-onset patients, especially those with a family history that is suggestive of LFS.

germline BRACA1, BRACA2 and TP53 mutation screening is warranted in early-onset Asian breast cancer patients, and that the presence of early breast cancer in the absence of LFS-linked cancer in the family is not sufficient to warrant TP53 testing.

we identified germline BRAC1, BRCA 2 and TP53 in 11%, 5% and 6% of early-onset (≤ 35 year old) breast cancer patients in a multi-ethic Asian cohort and that we found that TP53 mutation carriers had a family history of early-onset cancers (breast or LFS-associated cancers) in 75% of cases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying the genetic basis for breast cancer in a multi-ethical cohort.
the identification of germline TP 53 mutations in a cohort of 100 early-onset breast cancers.
the identification of genetic risk factors for breast cancer in Malaysia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of early breast cancer is an insufficient selection criteria for TP53 testing.
a germline TP3 mutation screening should be offered to early-onset patients with LFS features.

the presence of early onset breast cancer is an adequate selection criteria for TP53 mutation screening, but a detailed family history of LFC-linked cancers is required to identify the majority of TP53 mutation carriers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of early onset breast cancer alone is not a reliable selection criterion for TP53 testing in Asian breast cancer patients.
in low-resource settings, where family history is difficult to obtain, TP53 screening should only be offered to patients with a family or personal history of LFS-related cancers.
in a multi-ethnical Asian population, the frequency of germline BRAC1, BRAC2 and TP53 mutation is similar in early-onset (≤ 35) breast cancer patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the clinical utility of TP53 mutation screening may be improved by screening patients with a family cancer history suggestive of LFS, rather than early-onset breast cancers alone.
TP53 testing is not indicated in the absence of LFS or LFL features and should be reserved for patients with early-onsey breast cancer and LFS or LFS-like features.
TP53 mutation testing should be considered for early-onset breast cancers with a strong family history of breast cancers, sarcomas or brain tumors.
